newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EMU spells competition for futures exchanges - BIS.
newsitem.headline: EMU spells competition for futures exchanges - BIS.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said on Wednesday that futures exchanges will remain in stiff competition for market share as a result of impending European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"More confident expectations regarding the transition to the single European currency further intensified the debate concerning the likely consolidation of the European derivatives industry and about which of the major exchanges, products and technologies would gain supremacy in the new integrated environment," the Basle-based BIS said in its third-quarter report.

"The closure of the Irish Futures and Options Exchange (IFOX) in August, as well as the difficulties faced by a number of other European derivatives exchanges, have brought the potential consolidation facing the industry into sharp focus," it added.
It also said that the nature of instruments traded as EMU and the single currency are phased in is likely to change and will probably reduce the scope for existing contracts.

"With exchange rate and inflation risks ceasing to be prime determinants of returns on European fixed income securities, much trading activity will be conditioned by credit risk considerations," BIS said.
It expected the range of bond products to be reduced, with business instead going to the cash underlying markets.
Competition was expected to be fierce for volume in short-term interest rate contracts.
The BIS noted that "eurocurrency rates are based on generic interbank rates and will therefore not be able to support much more than a few pan-European short-term contracts."

The BIS also noted that both the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) and the German futures exchange Deutsche Terminboerse (DTB) announced in November that they were launching one-month euromark contracts.
"Increased activity in German mark interest rate swaps and greater issuance of short-term paper by the Bundesbank could support activity in those contracts," the BIS said.
It said that differences in national accounting, disclosure and fiscal treatment within the new currency area were likely to shield the European equity products from some competion.
As to the location, the BIS said that "the emergence of a dominant trading location will not be conditioned by a single advantage but will depend on a complex set of interrelated factors."
